tier_reason: The blog post (2026-08-18, by Han Liu, Head of Kafka & Fluss at Rednote, presented at Flink Forward Asia 2026) gives only relative production figures against the prior Kafka pipeline: about 3x peak throughput, 30-90% bandwidth savings, about 30% lower write CPU, about 50% less write traffic, and 50-80% faster index builds. It has no absolute numbers, hardware, benchmark code or methodology beyond a mention of 'load tests against the critical Kafka baselines', so this is C.

corrections.workload: rednote (Xiaohongshu) production migration of a core real-time search/recommendation/ads indexing pipeline from Kafka to Fluss: wide tables consumed by many downstream services with 1x to about 1000x fan-out. It uses Arrow columnar writes with column pruning and direct object-store/Paimon (Lakestream) reads for cold-data scans. One table ingests about 1 billion records / 10 TB per day.
corrections.caveats: The case study is written by the end user (Rednote's Head of Kafka & Fluss) but published on the Fluss project's own blog. It gives only self-reported relative percentages and multipliers, with no absolute throughput, hardware or methodology. The page says the migration changed data layout, access paths and workload isolation at the same time, so the gains come from column pruning on wide high-fan-out tables and from isolating cold reads, not from a like-for-like broker benchmark.

notes: All claimed numbers appear verbatim on the page, and the metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 2184 stars, last commit 2026-09-24, not archived or a fork. I only refined workload and caveats to say that the win depends on the workload's columnar/fan-out pattern.

tier_reason: This is a vendor-run (StreamNative, 2022-04-07) Linux Foundation OpenMessaging Benchmark comparison. The page links the public workload and driver files in github.com/openmessaging/benchmark (workloads/1-topic-100-partitions-1kb-4p-4c-*.yaml, driver-pulsar/pulsar.yaml, driver-kafka/kafka-*.yaml), but hardware is given only as AWS instance types with no CPU model. That makes it first-party numbers short of A, so C, which matches how the vendor OMB run for Redpanda was graded in batch-08.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Max throughput at 100 partitions: Pulsar without journaling 1600MB/s vs Kafka 1087MB/s (~1.47x, derived from page data). Default Pulsar with journaling reached 800MB/s, which is below Kafka. Single partition: Pulsar 700MB/s without journal / 580MB/s with journal vs Kafka 280MB/s (~2.5x, derived from page data); the page headlines this as '2.5x maximum throughput'. P99 publish latency at a fixed 500MB/s: Pulsar without journal 1.58ms, with journal 7.89ms, vs Kafka 3.46ms. Kafka's P99.9 was 54.56ms, and the page says both Pulsar configs beat Kafka at P99.9 and above, headlining '100x lower than Kafka at P99.99'. Catch-up reads from a 512GB backlog: Pulsar up to 3.2GB/s vs Kafka 2.0GB/s ('60% more'; headline '1.5x faster historical read rate'). Pulsar drained the backlog ~2.5x faster, while Kafka producers' P99 rose to ~700ms.
corrections.workload: Linux Foundation OpenMessaging Benchmark with 1KB messages on 3 broker VMs (i3en.6xlarge) and 4 client VMs (m5n.8xlarge) on AWS. Tests: max throughput with 1 and 100 partitions, publish latency at a fixed 500MB/s on 100 partitions, and catch-up read throughput draining a 512GB backlog while producers keep writing.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark was run and published by StreamNative, whose CTO co-created Pulsar, so it is a vendor-interested comparison rather than an independent third party, even though it uses the public OMB suite. It is dated (2022-04-07; Pulsar 2.9.1 vs Kafka 3.0.0). Default Pulsar (journaling, fsync before ack) loses to Kafka on 100-partition max throughput (800 vs 1087MB/s) and on P99 latency (7.89 vs 3.46ms). The 'equivalent durability' wins use the non-default no-journal config, and Kafka used Confluent's OMB-recommended config with no fsync before ack. Hardware is given as AWS instance types, not a CPU model.

notes: The record put '~2.5x' on the 100-partition 1600 vs 1087MB/s pair, which is really ~1.47x. The page's 2.5x headline comes from the single-partition test (700 vs 280MB/s), so I fixed claimed_speedup. I also caught the '3.2GB/s vs 2.0GB/s' catch-up claim, which is on the page. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 15338 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not archived or a fork.

tier_reason: The numbers are CI-bot reports (github-actions, 2024-06-13 to 2024-07-08) in AutoMQ's own OMB fork (AutoMQ/kafka-provider-comparison: workflow_scripts/, driver-automq, driver-kafka, .github/workflows/prepare-vs-benchmark.yml). The code is public, but the issue never states instance or CPU model, so these are first-party numbers with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: At a fixed 500MB/s (128000 msg/s x 4KB, 1000 partitions): pub latency avg 3.4ms vs Kafka 4.2ms and P99 15.19ms vs 30.21ms (2024-06-13 run). Later 500MB/s runs gave P99 15.69 vs 37.65ms and 14.6 vs 40.48ms. At ~100MB/s (25600 msg/s): avg/P99 8.08/30.62ms vs Kafka 17.98/75.13ms (2024-06-24) and 6.81/25.36ms vs 12.3/72.54ms (2024-07-08). E2E latency was mixed: in the 2024-06-13 run Kafka had lower E2E avg (6.31 vs 6.54ms) and P95 (12.39 vs 15.91ms), while AutoMQ had lower E2E P99 (34.16 vs 42.31ms). In two 1-minute smoke runs at producerRate 100, AutoMQ had higher avg pub latency (3.05 vs 2.54ms, 2.71 vs 2.28ms). The fixed producerRate pinned throughput equal. Estimated total cost at 500MB/s was $2373.35 for AutoMQ vs $10647.35 for Kafka.
corrections.hardware: AWS EC2 via the repo's driver-*/deploy/aws-cn Terraform. The issue never states instance types per run, and var.tfvars changed during the run series (2024-06-12 'use free tier', 2024-06-20 'use small size'; currently r6i.large). replicationFactor was 1 for AutoMQ and 3 for Kafka.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo (AutoMQ/kafka-provider-comparison, an OMB fork) is AutoMQ-authored, and its last commit was 2024-07-12. It is abandoned as a comparison tool even though AutoMQ itself is active. The instance or CPU model is not stated and changed during the run series. The shared topic config sets flush.messages=1 (fsync per message, a non-default setting that penalizes Kafka's latency), and replication is asymmetric (AutoMQ RF=1 on shared storage vs Kafka RF=3). Throughput was capped by producerRate, so this is a latency/cost claim, not a throughput-speedup claim, and E2E results were mixed. AutoMQ is a source fork of Apache Kafka, so the baseline is its own upstream.

notes: The claimed pub-latency and cost numbers match the bot comments on issue #1 exactly. I added the mixed E2E and low-rate results and the flush.messages=1 config, which likely handicaps Kafka. The README says 'AutoMQ is a fork of the open-source Apache Kafka', so I set is_fork_of (it is not a GitHub fork). The rest of the metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 10872 stars, last commit 2026-09-24.
